name: Anubis, the Jackal Who Weighs Your Heart
scope: The black jackal-headed god who embalmed the dead and stood at the scales in the Hall of Judgment; the dead person's heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at, and if it was heavier, the monster Ammit devoured it. Anubis invented mummification when he wrapped Osiris.
source: Britannica: Anubis; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology (Handbook of the Gods)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, Egyptian tradition presented straight and seriously. Answer = the named god (Anubis) or the vivid act (the heart weighed against a feather; Ammit waiting to devour). The scales-of-judgment image is the Dinner-Test hook; the black-jackal-as-embalmer is the concrete handle.

name: Bastet, the Cat Goddess of Bubastis
scope: The goddess of home, protection, and cats, worshipped at Bubastis; began as a fierce lioness and softened into a cat over centuries; her festival drew huge river-boat crowds (Herodotus). Cats were so sacred that harming one could be a capital crime.
source: Britannica: Bastet; Herodotus, Histories II; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology
framing_note: Scene-led, symmetric respect. Answer = the named goddess (Bastet) or the vivid turn (a lioness who became a house cat; killing a cat could cost a life). Keep it wondrous, not smug about 'cat worship.'

name: Sobek, the Crocodile God of the Nile
scope: The crocodile-headed god of the Nile's power, military might, and fertility; his cult center at Faiyum (Crocodilopolis) kept a living sacred crocodile decked in gold and jewels named Petsuchos, replaced when it died.
source: Britannica: Sobek; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology; Strabo, Geographica XVII
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = Sobek, or the vivid detail (a real crocodile wearing gold jewelry as a living god). The jeweled temple crocodile is the memorable handle.

name: Sekhmet, the Lioness of War and Plague
scope: The lion-headed goddess whose breath was the desert wind and whose fury nearly destroyed humanity; Ra tricked her into drinking beer dyed red like blood until she fell asleep and calmed into gentle Hathor. Her name means 'the Powerful One.'
source: Britannica: Sekhmet; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology; the Book of the Heavenly Cow
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Sekhmet, or the vivid story (blood-red beer tricks the rampaging lioness into peace). The beer-flood myth is the Dinner-Test payoff. Balance to Bastet — same species, opposite mood.

name: Thoth, the Ibis Who Invented Writing
scope: The ibis-headed (sometimes baboon) god of writing, wisdom, and the moon; he recorded the verdict at the weighing of the heart and was credited with inventing hieroglyphs. The curved ibis beak echoes the scribe's reed pen.
source: Britannica: Thoth; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology
framing_note: Scene-led. Answer = Thoth, or the vivid role (the god who recorded the soul's verdict, inventor of writing). The ibis-beak-as-pen link is the concrete handle. Pairs naturally with the Anubis scales ladder.

name: Horus the Falcon and the Eye of Horus
scope: The falcon-headed sky god of kingship; every pharaoh was Horus on the throne; he lost an eye battling Set to avenge his father Osiris, and the restored Eye of Horus became a protective amulet (and the source of the modern Rx symbol legend).
source: Britannica: Horus; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Horus, or the vivid image (the falcon god who lost an eye avenging his murdered father; the eye became the protective amulet). Keep the Set-vs-Horus feud concrete.

name: Apis, the Living Sacred Bull of Memphis
scope: A single living bull chosen by strict markings (a white triangle on the forehead, a scarab shape under the tongue) was worshipped as a god at Memphis; when it died it was mummified and entombed in the vast Serapeum, and priests searched for its successor.
source: Britannica: Apis; Serapeum of Saqqara excavation records (Mariette)
framing_note: Scene-led. Answer = Apis, or the vivid detail (a real bull chosen by secret markings, buried in a giant stone tomb). The Serapeum of granite sarcophagi is the wonder handle.

name: Egypt's Millions of Mummified Cats
scope: Cats were bred at temples specifically to be mummified as offerings to Bastet; one 1888 find at Beni Hasan uncovered an estimated 80,000+ cat mummies, so many that a shipment was ground up for fertilizer in England. Killing a cat could be a capital offense.
source: Britannica: animal mummies of Egypt; Ikram, Divine Creatures: Animal Mummies in Ancient Egypt
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = the vivid number/fact (tens of thousands of cat mummies, some sold as fertilizer). The fertilizer-shipment detail is the Dinner-Test payoff — strange but true, not mocking.

name: Pegasus, the Winged Horse Born of Blood
scope: The white winged horse who sprang from Medusa's neck when Perseus beheaded her; the hero Bellerophon tamed him with Athena's golden bridle and rode him to slay the fire-breathing Chimera, then was thrown when he tried to fly to Olympus. Pegasus became a constellation.
source: Britannica: Pegasus; Hesiod, Theogony; Apollodorus, Library
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the named creature (Pegasus) or the vivid origin (born from Medusa's severed neck). Bellerophon's fall for overreaching is the memorable moral beat. Keep names as context, not 'who rode Pegasus' cold trivia.

name: Cerberus, the Three-Headed Hound of Hades
scope: The three-headed dog with a serpent tail who guarded the gates of the underworld, letting the dead in but never out; Heracles' twelfth and final labor was to drag him up to the living world bare-handed. Orpheus lulled him to sleep with music.
source: Britannica: Cerberus; Apollodorus, Library; Hesiod, Theogony
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Cerberus, or the vivid feat (dragging the underworld guard-dog to the surface with bare hands; Orpheus singing him to sleep). Keep the labor concrete.

name: The Minotaur in the Labyrinth of Crete
scope: The bull-headed man imprisoned in Daedalus's maze beneath Knossos, fed a tribute of Athenian youths; Theseus killed him and found his way out by unspooling Ariadne's thread. The creature was born of King Minos's wife and a divine bull.
source: Britannica: Minotaur; Plutarch, Life of Theseus; Apollodorus, Library
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the Minotaur, or the vivid escape (following Ariadne's thread back out of the maze). The bull-in-a-labyrinth image is the Dinner-Test hook.

name: Centaurs and Chiron the Wise Tutor
scope: Half-man, half-horse beings, mostly wild and violent (they brawled drunk at a wedding) — except Chiron, immortal healer and teacher who trained Achilles, Jason, and Asclepius; wounded by a poisoned arrow, he gave up his immortality to end the pain and became a constellation.
source: Britannica: Centaur; Apollodorus, Library; Pindar
framing_note: Scene-led. Answer = the centaur / Chiron, or the vivid contrast (savage brawlers vs. the one wise healer who tutored heroes). Chiron trading immortality to escape agony is the emotional T4 beat.

name: The Nemean Lion and the Hydra: Heracles' First Labors
scope: The Nemean Lion's hide was impervious to weapons, so Heracles strangled it and wore its skin ever after; the Lernaean Hydra grew two heads for every one cut off until he cauterized each stump with fire. Two of the twelve labors, both about a monster that can't be beaten the obvious way.
source: Britannica: Labours of Heracles; Apollodorus, Library
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the named beast (Nemean Lion / Hydra) or the clever solution (strangle what blades can't cut; burn the Hydra's stumps). The 'can't-win-normally' twist is the payoff.

name: The Roman Eagle: Aquila of the Legions
scope: The silver (later gold) eagle standard carried by every Roman legion, sacred to Jupiter; to lose the aquila in battle was the ultimate disgrace, and Rome mounted whole campaigns to recover eagles lost by Varus in the Teutoburg Forest. The aquilifer who carried it was a soldier of honor.
source: Britannica: aquila (Roman standard); Tacitus, Annals; Cassius Dio
framing_note: Scene-led. Answer = the eagle standard (aquila), or the vivid stakes (losing the eagle was a national shame worth a war to reverse). The lost-eagles-of-Teutoburg detail is the Dinner-Test handle.

name: Reading the Gods in a Sheep's Liver: Roman Haruspicy
scope: Etruscan-trained priests (haruspices) foretold the future by inspecting the entrails, especially the liver, of sacrificed animals; a surviving bronze model liver from Piacenza is mapped into named regions for reading omens. A blemished liver could halt a battle or an election.
source: Britannica: haruspices; the Piacenza Liver (Etruscan bronze); Cicero, De Divinatione
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition presented straight (not as superstition to sneer at). Answer = the practice (reading a liver for omens) or the vivid artifact (the bronze Piacenza liver map). Keep it wondrous.

name: The She-Wolf Who Suckled Romulus and Remus
scope: The founding legend of Rome: abandoned twin infants set adrift on the Tiber were found and nursed by a she-wolf (the Lupa) in a cave, then raised by a shepherd; Romulus later founded the city. The she-wolf became Rome's emblem.
source: Britannica: Romulus and Remus; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita I; the Capitoline Wolf
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the she-wolf (Lupa) or the vivid image (a wolf nursing the two babies who would found Rome). The animal at the heart of a city's origin is the hook.

name: Sleipnir, Odin's Eight-Legged Horse
scope: The gray eight-legged steed who carried Odin across the sky and down to the land of the dead; born when Loki, disguised as a mare, lured away the giant builder's stallion Svadilfari — making Loki the horse's mother. The fastest horse in the Nine Worlds.
source: Britannica: Sleipnir; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Sleipnir, or the vivid origin (Loki turned into a mare and gave birth to Odin's horse). Eight legs and the shapeshifting birth are the Dinner-Test payoffs.

name: Huginn and Muninn, Odin's Spy Ravens
scope: The two ravens 'Thought' and 'Memory' who fly across the whole world every dawn and return to whisper the news into Odin's ears; Odin admits he fears more for Muninn (Memory) not coming back. Ravens circling a battlefield were seen as Odin's own.
source: Britannica: Huginn and Muninn; Poetic Edda (Grimnismal); Snorri, Prose Edda
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the named ravens (Huginn and Muninn / Thought and Memory) or the vivid act (they fly the world daily and report back). Odin fearing to lose Memory is the poignant beat.

name: Fenrir, the Wolf Chained Until Ragnarok
scope: Loki's monstrous wolf-son who grew so fast the gods feared him; they bound him with the impossibly-soft magic ribbon Gleipnir made of six impossible things, but only after Tyr placed his hand in Fenrir's jaws as a pledge — and lost it. At Ragnarok, Fenrir breaks free and swallows Odin.
source: Britannica: Fenrir; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Fenrir, or the vivid sacrifice (Tyr gave his hand into the wolf's mouth so the gods could chain it). The soft ribbon made of impossible things and the doom of swallowing Odin are the deep-tier payoffs.

name: Jormungandr, the World Serpent
scope: Loki's serpent-child, flung into the ocean, grew so vast it circles the whole world and bites its own tail; Thor once hooked it while fishing with an ox-head bait and nearly hauled it up. At Ragnarok, Thor kills it but dies from its venom after nine steps.
source: Britannica: Jormungandr; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda; Poetic Edda (Hymiskvida)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Jormungandr (the World Serpent) or the vivid image (a snake so huge it wraps the world biting its tail; Thor fishing for it). Thor's mutual doom with the serpent is the T4 beat.

name: Ratatoskr, the Gossip Squirrel of the World Tree
scope: The squirrel who scurries up and down the trunk of the world-tree Yggdrasil, carrying spiteful insults between the eagle perched at the top and the dragon Nidhogg gnawing at the root — deliberately stirring up their feud.
source: Britannica: Yggdrasil; Snorri, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning); Poetic Edda (Grimnismal)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Ratatoskr, or the vivid role (a squirrel running messages of insults up and down the world tree). The gossip-carrier detail is the Dinner-Test hook.

name: Audhumla, the Cow Who Licked the First God from Ice
scope: In the Norse creation, the primordial cow Audhumla fed the frost-giant Ymir with her four rivers of milk, and over three days licked a salty ice-block until the first god, Buri (Odin's grandfather), emerged — hair, then head, then whole man.
source: Britannica: Audhumla; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Audhumla, or the vivid act (a cow licking a god out of the ice over three days). The cow-at-the-start-of-creation is the memorable handle.

name: Thor's Goats That Die for Dinner and Rise Again
scope: Thor's chariot is pulled by two goats, Tanngrisnir and Tanngnjostr, whom he can slaughter and eat each night — then resurrect whole the next morning by blessing the bones with his hammer, provided no bone was cracked. A farm-boy cracked one for the marrow and left a goat lame.
source: Britannica: Thor; Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda (Gylfaginning)
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the resurrecting goats, or the vivid rule (eat them at night, they live again at dawn — unless you crack a bone). The marrow-cracking mistake is the Dinner-Test twist.

name: Hanuman, the Monkey God Who Leapt to Lanka
scope: The mighty monkey (vanara) devotee of Rama who leapt across the ocean to Lanka to find the captive Sita, and when told to fetch one healing herb, carried back the entire mountain because he couldn't tell which plant it was. The model of selfless devotion.
source: Britannica: Hanuman; Valmiki, Ramayana
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition presented straight and reverently. Answer = Hanuman, or the vivid feat (leaping the sea; carrying a whole mountain to be sure of the healing herb). Devotion is the emotional spine; keep it wondrous, not doctrinal.

name: Ganesha, the Elephant-Headed Remover of Obstacles
scope: The elephant-headed god of beginnings and remover of obstacles; his father Shiva beheaded him not recognizing him and replaced the head with an elephant's; he rides a tiny mouse, and broke off his own tusk to use as a pen to write down the Mahabharata.
source: Britannica: Ganesha; the Puranas; the Mahabharata frame-story
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = Ganesha, or the vivid detail (elephant head on a boy's body; an elephant god who rides a mouse; the tusk-pen). The mismatched mount and the broken tusk are the Dinner-Test payoffs.

name: Nandi, Shiva's Bull Who Always Faces the Shrine
scope: Shiva's white bull mount and gatekeeper; in nearly every Shiva temple a stone Nandi sits patiently facing the inner sanctum, and worshippers whisper their wishes into his ear to carry to the god. The symbol of steady devotion and dharma.
source: Britannica: Nandi; Shaiva temple tradition
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight. Answer = Nandi, or the vivid custom (whispering wishes into the stone bull's ear so he'll tell Shiva). The always-facing-the-shrine detail is the memorable handle.

name: Garuda, Vishnu's Eagle and Enemy of Serpents
scope: The great eagle mount of Vishnu, sworn enemy of the naga serpents; born to free his enslaved mother, he stole the elixir of immortality from the gods themselves. He appears as a national emblem of Indonesia and Thailand today.
source: Britannica: Garuda; the Mahabharata (Adi Parva); Indonesian/Thai national symbols
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = Garuda, or the vivid deed (the eagle who stole the nectar of immortality to free his mother). The snake-enemy and the living national-emblem detail are handles.

name: Gau Mata: The Sacred Cow of Hinduism
scope: The cow as 'Mother' (Gau Mata), source of milk and gentleness, honored and protected; the wish-fulfilling cow Kamadhenu in myth is said to contain all the gods in her body. Cow protection remains a living and politically charged practice in India today.
source: Britannica: sanctity of the cow in Hinduism; Kamadhenu in the Puranas
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition presented straight and respectfully. Answer = the sacred cow / Kamadhenu, or the vivid image (a cow said to hold all the gods within her). Note the modern significance factually without preaching.

name: Nagas: The Serpent Deities Who Guard the Waters
scope: Semi-divine serpent beings, depicted with a many-headed cobra hood, who guard treasures and waters; the great serpent Shesha (Ananta) coils beneath Vishnu as his cosmic couch, and a naga hood shelters the meditating Buddha in later tradition too.
source: Britannica: naga; the Puranas; pan-Indian iconography
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = the naga / Shesha, or the vivid image (the world-serpent as Vishnu's bed; a cobra hood sheltering a god). Keep it reverent and concrete.

name: The Chinese Zodiac and the Great Race
scope: The twelve animals — Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat, Monkey, Rooster, Dog, Pig — and the Jade Emperor's river race that set their order: the clever Rat rode the Ox's head and leapt off at the finish to win, and the Cat was cheated out of a place (some say the Rat never woke it).
source: Britannica: Chinese zodiac (shengxiao); traditional race legend
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition presented straight. Answer = the named animal or the vivid trick (the rat riding then leaping off the ox to win; why the cat is missing). Deep ladder: race order at low tiers, individual animals' traits and the missing-cat mystery deeper. No rote 'list the zodiac' — always via story.

name: The Chinese Dragon: Rain-Bringer, Not Monster
scope: The Chinese dragon (long) is a benevolent water-and-sky spirit that brings rain and prosperity — the opposite of the fire-breathing Western villain; it has the body of nine animals, the emperor sat on the 'Dragon Throne,' and only he could wear the five-clawed dragon.
source: Britannica: Chinese dragon (long); imperial iconography
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, symmetric respect. Answer = the Chinese dragon, or the vivid contrast (a good luck-bringing rain dragon vs. the Western evil dragon; the emperor's five-clawed monopoly). The nine-animal composite is a concrete handle.

name: The Fenghuang, China's Phoenix
scope: The fenghuang, a radiant composite bird of peace and virtue that appears only in times of harmony and good rule; paired with the dragon as the female-and-male / empress-and-emperor symbol, it is often (loosely) called the Chinese phoenix.
source: Britannica: fenghuang; Chinese imperial symbolism
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight. Answer = the fenghuang, or the vivid role (the bird that appears only when the realm is at peace; paired with the dragon as empress to emperor). Keep the dragon-phoenix pairing concrete.

name: The White Tiger of the West and the Four Symbols
scope: The four celestial guardians of the sky's directions: the Azure Dragon of the East, the Vermilion Bird of the South, the White Tiger of the West, and the Black Tortoise (entwined with a snake) of the North — each a constellation quarter and a season.
source: Britannica: Four Symbols (Chinese constellations); classical astronomy
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = the named guardian (White Tiger of the West, etc.) or the vivid image (four beast-constellations guarding the four directions). The tortoise-and-snake North is the odd, memorable one.

name: The Thunderbird, Whose Wings Make the Storm
scope: A vast supernatural bird known across many North American peoples; the beat of its wings is thunder and lightning flashes from its eyes; in Pacific Northwest tradition it wars with the underwater serpent, and it is carved atop totem poles.
source: Britannica: Thunderbird (mythology); Pacific Northwest and Plains oral traditions
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition presented straight and seriously (no 'primitive myth' framing). Answer = the Thunderbird, or the vivid image (a bird whose wingbeats are thunder and whose eyes flash lightning). Attribute to the tradition broadly and respectfully.

name: Raven, the Trickster Who Stole the Sun
scope: In Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian tradition of the Pacific Northwest, Raven is both greedy trickster and world-shaper; he stole the sun, moon, and stars, which a chief hoarded in boxes, by transforming into a pine needle to be swallowed and reborn as the chief's grandson — then released the light to the world.
source: Britannica: Raven (trickster); Tlingit/Haida/Tsimshian oral tradition
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight and serious. Answer = Raven, or the vivid trick (turning into a pine needle to be swallowed, then stealing the sun to give the world light). Name the peoples respectfully as context.

name: Coyote, the Trickster of the Plains and Southwest
scope: Coyote is the shape-shifting fool-and-sage of many Plains and Southwest peoples — sometimes a world-maker who scatters the stars in a careless moment, sometimes a greedy schemer whose plans backfire; the tales both entertain and teach how not to behave.
source: Britannica: Coyote (trickster); Navajo, Crow, and other oral traditions
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = Coyote, or the vivid role (the trickster whose blunder scatters the stars across the sky). Present the wise-fool duality respectfully, not as comic 'primitive' belief.

name: The Sacred Eagle and the Eagle Feather
scope: The eagle, flying highest and closest to the Creator, is sacred to most tribes; an eagle feather is earned through an act of honor, not bought, and worn ceremonially. US law uniquely permits enrolled tribal members to possess eagle feathers otherwise protected.
source: Britannica: eagle in Native American culture; National Eagle Repository
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition presented straight and respectfully. Answer = the eagle / the earned feather, or the vivid custom (a feather earned by an act of honor, never bought). Keep the animal and the honor central; touch the feather-law only as it bears on the bird's sacredness, not as statute-drill.

name: The Buffalo, Center of Plains Life
scope: The American bison was the whole economy and spirit of the Plains nations — meat, hide for tipis and robes, sinew for thread, bone for tools, and a sacred being honored in the White Buffalo Calf Woman story of the Lakota, who brought the sacred pipe.
source: Britannica: bison and Plains cultures; Lakota White Buffalo Calf Woman tradition
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = the buffalo/bison, or the vivid use (nearly every part of the animal became food, shelter, or tool) and the White Buffalo Calf Woman story. Keep the reverence and the near-total use central; the population collapse belongs to Pillar 4, so keep the animal-in-culture the focus here.

name: Bear Medicine and the Healer's Spirit
scope: In many tribes the bear stands for healing, strength, and introspection; because bears dig up medicinal roots and disappear into winter dens to re-emerge, they are linked to renewal and to the medicine societies that healed the sick.
source: Britannica: bear symbolism in Native American cultures; ethnographic sources
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight and respectful. Answer = the bear / bear medicine, or the vivid link (the animal that digs up healing roots and 'dies' into its den to be reborn each spring). Keep it wondrous and specific.

name: The Lamb of God and the Agnus Dei
scope: Christ as the sacrificial lamb: John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world,' fulfilling the Passover lamb whose blood spared the Israelites; the Agnus Dei image shows a lamb bearing a banner of victory.
source: Britannica: Agnus Dei; Gospel of John 1:29; Exodus (Passover)
framing_note: Scene-led, Christian tradition presented straight and on the same plane as the others — no privileging, no slighting. Answer = the Lamb of God, or the vivid link (the Passover lamb's blood fulfilled in Christ). Keep the symbol concrete.

name: The Dove of the Holy Spirit
scope: At Jesus' baptism the Spirit descends 'like a dove'; earlier, the dove Noah released returns with an olive leaf, signaling the flood's end and the making of peace. The dove becomes the enduring symbol of the Spirit and of peace.
source: Britannica: dove as Christian symbol; Genesis 8 (Noah); Gospel accounts of the Baptism
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight, same plane as the others. Answer = the dove, or the vivid scene (the olive-leaf-bearing dove ending the flood; the Spirit descending at the baptism). Keep it concrete.

name: The Lion of Judah
scope: The lion as the emblem of the tribe of Judah, applied to Christ as the conquering king ('the Lion of the tribe of Judah has triumphed,' Revelation 5:5); the same passage pairs the lion with the slain lamb — power revealed through sacrifice.
source: Britannica: Lion of Judah; Genesis 49 (Jacob's blessing); Revelation 5
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight, on the same plane. Answer = the Lion of Judah, or the vivid pairing (the conquering lion who turns out to be the slain lamb). Keep the symbol concrete.

name: The Ichthys: The Secret Fish of the Early Church
scope: The simple two-arc fish drawn by early Christians under Roman persecution; the Greek word ICHTHYS ('fish') was read as an acrostic — Jesus Christ, God's Son, Savior — and served as a covert sign, one person drawing an arc, the other completing it to identify a fellow believer.
source: Britannica: ichthys (Christian symbol); early-church catacomb inscriptions
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight, same plane. Answer = the fish / ichthys, or the vivid use (a secret sign completed between two people to identify a Christian under persecution). The acrostic and the covert handshake are the payoffs.

name: The Four Living Creatures of the Evangelists
scope: The winged man, lion, ox, and eagle of Ezekiel's vision and Revelation, matched by tradition to the four Gospel writers: Matthew the man, Mark the lion, Luke the ox, and John the eagle — a tetramorph carved and painted across cathedrals.
source: Britannica: tetramorph / Four Evangelists symbols; Ezekiel 1; Revelation 4
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight, same plane. Answer = the matched creature (Mark the lion, John the eagle, etc.) or the vivid source (four winged beasts of Ezekiel's throne-vision). Keep the man-lion-ox-eagle set concrete.

name: The Serpent in Eden and the Bronze Serpent of Moses
scope: The serpent as the deceiver in the Garden of Eden — and, surprisingly, its opposite: when snakes plague the Israelites, Moses raises a bronze serpent on a pole and any who look at it live, read in Christian tradition as a foreshadowing of the cross.
source: Britannica: serpent symbolism; Genesis 3; Numbers 21; Gospel of John 3
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight, same plane. Answer = the serpent, or the vivid reversal (the same animal that deceived in Eden becomes the healing bronze serpent lifted on a pole). The tempter-vs-healer twist is the hook.

name: The Peacock and the Pelican: Medieval Christian Beasts
scope: The peacock, whose flesh was believed never to rot, stood for resurrection and its hundred-eyed tail for an all-seeing God; the pelican, believed to pierce its own breast to feed its young with its blood, became a symbol of Christ's self-sacrifice. Both from the medieval bestiaries.
source: Britannica: bestiary; medieval Physiologus tradition
framing_note: Scene-led, tradition straight, same plane. Answer = the named bird and its meaning (peacock = incorruptible resurrection; pelican = self-sacrifice). The 'flesh that never rots' and the self-wounding pelican are the Dinner-Test payoffs, presented as the belief held (bestiary lore), not as fact.

name: Bucephalus, the Horse Only Alexander Could Tame
scope: The great black stallion no one could ride until the boy Alexander noticed the horse was terrified of its own shadow, turned it to face the sun, and mounted it; Bucephalus carried him across an empire to India, and Alexander founded a city, Bucephala, in the horse's memory when it died.
source: Britannica: Bucephalus; Plutarch, Life of Alexander; Arrian, Anabasis
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story told straight. Answer = Bucephalus, or the vivid insight (a boy spotting that the wild horse feared its own shadow). The city named for the horse is the T4 payoff.

name: Hannibal's War Elephants Over the Alps
scope: In 218 BC Hannibal marched ~37 war elephants across the freezing Alps to invade Italy; most died on the crossing or soon after, but the few survivors terrified Roman soldiers and horses who had never seen such beasts. One elephant, Surus, was said to be his favorite.
source: Britannica: Hannibal; Polybius, Histories; Livy, Ab Urbe Condita
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = the war elephants over the Alps, or the vivid image (elephants freezing on a mountain pass to terrify Rome). Keep the animal central, not the campaign logistics.

name: Incitatus, Caligula's Horse Almost Made Consul
scope: The emperor Caligula lavished his favorite racehorse Incitatus with a marble stall, an ivory manger, purple blankets, and a jeweled collar, invited it to dinner, and — the Romans said — planned to make it a consul. Whether he truly meant to is a scandal reported by Suetonius, uncertain as history.
source: Britannica: Caligula; Suetonius, Lives of the Caesars; Cassius Dio
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, told straight but honest about the uncertainty. Answer = Incitatus, or the vivid pampering (a horse with a marble stall and an invitation to dinner). Flag the consul story as a reported rumor, not confirmed fact.

name: Marengo, the Horse Who Carried Napoleon
scope: The small gray Arabian stallion said to have carried Napoleon through Austerlitz, Jena, Wagram, and the retreat from Waterloo, wounded many times yet always steady under fire; captured by the British after Waterloo, his skeleton is still displayed in London.
source: Britannica: Napoleon's horse Marengo; National Army Museum, London
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight (noting some accounts blur the legend). Answer = Marengo, or the vivid fact (the little Arabian who carried Napoleon through his great battles; his skeleton still on show). The surviving skeleton is the payoff.

name: Sergeant Stubby, the Most Decorated Dog of WWI
scope: A stray Boston terrier mix smuggled to the trenches of France, Stubby learned to warn his unit of gas attacks by smell before the men could sense it, found wounded soldiers in no-man's-land, and once held a German infiltrator by the seat of his pants until help came — earning him a sergeant's rank.
source: Britannica: Sergeant Stubby; Smithsonian National Museum of American History
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = Stubby, or the vivid deed (smelling gas before the men could; catching a spy by the trousers). The gas-warning and spy-capture are the Dinner-Test payoffs.

name: Hachiko, the Dog Who Waited Nine Years
scope: The Akita who met his professor every evening at Tokyo's Shibuya Station — and, after the professor died suddenly at work in 1925, returned to the same spot at the same time each day for nine more years until his own death. A bronze statue of him stands at Shibuya today.
source: Britannica: Hachiko; contemporary Japanese newspaper accounts; Shibuya statue
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight, emotionally plain (no over-anthropomorphizing beyond the documented waiting). Answer = Hachiko, or the vivid fact (nine years of waiting at the same station for a man who would never come). The bronze statue is the T3 handle.

name: Laika, the First Living Being in Orbit
scope: A gentle Moscow street dog chosen by the Soviets for Sputnik 2 in November 1957, becoming the first animal to orbit Earth; the capsule had no way to return her, and she died of overheating within hours — a fact only fully admitted decades later.
source: Britannica: Laika; Soviet space program records; later Russian disclosures
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight and honest (including the one-way nature and the later admission). Answer = Laika, or the vivid fact (a street dog became the first creature to orbit Earth, with no way home). Handle the death factually and soberly, not sentimentally.

name: Cher Ami, the Pigeon Who Saved the Lost Battalion
scope: A carrier pigeon of WWI who, shot through the breast with a leg nearly torn off, flew ~25 miles in about 25 minutes carrying the message that stopped friendly artillery from shelling the trapped 'Lost Battalion'; 194 of the surrounded men survived. Cher Ami earned the Croix de Guerre and is preserved at the Smithsonian.
source: Britannica: Cher Ami; Smithsonian National Museum of American History
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = Cher Ami, or the vivid flight (a gravely wounded pigeon flying the message that saved the surrounded battalion). Note the lost-leg and message as documented; treat the popular 'lost an eye' detail cautiously (photos dispute it) — don't assert it as fact.

name: Wojtek, the Bear Who Carried Shells at Monte Cassino
scope: A Syrian brown bear cub bought from a boy in Iran and raised by Polish soldiers, who officially enlisted him as a private (later corporal) in the 22nd Artillery Supply Company so he could travel by troopship; at Monte Cassino in 1944 he carried heavy crates of artillery shells and never dropped one. He retired to Edinburgh Zoo.
source: Britannica: Wojtek the Bear; Imperial War Museum accounts
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = Wojtek, or the vivid fact (an enlisted bear who hauled artillery shells in battle). The 22nd Company adopted a bear-carrying-a-shell as its emblem — a great handle.

name: Smoky, the Four-Pound Yorkie of the Pacific War
scope: A tiny Yorkshire terrier found in a New Guinea foxhole who served with US forces in the Pacific; her most famous feat was pulling a telegraph wire through a 70-foot pipe under an airfield, saving days of digging, and she is remembered as an early war therapy dog.
source: Britannica / Smithsonian on Smoky the war dog; Wynne, Yorkie Doodle Dandy
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = Smoky, or the vivid feat (a four-pound dog dragging a wire through a 70-foot pipe to save an airfield's crews from digging). Keep the size-vs-feat contrast central.

name: Balto and Togo: The 1925 Serum Run to Nome
scope: When diphtheria threatened Nome, Alaska in 1925, teams of sled dogs relayed lifesaving serum across ~674 miles of blizzard; Togo, Leonhard Seppala's lead dog, ran by far the longest and most dangerous leg, while Balto, who ran the short final stretch into Nome, got the statue in New York and the fame.
source: Britannica: 1925 serum run to Nome; contemporary accounts of Togo and Balto
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = the named dog (Togo did the hardest leg; Balto got the fame) or the vivid relay (sled dogs racing serum through a blizzard to a dying town). The Togo-did-the-work / Balto-got-the-glory contrast is the payoff.

name: Trigger, the Smartest Horse in the Movies
scope: Roy Rogers' golden palomino stallion, billed as 'the Smartest Horse in the Movies,' who could perform dozens of tricks; when Trigger died Rogers had him preserved by taxidermy and mounted, rearing, on display at his museum.
source: Britannica / entertainment histories of Roy Rogers and Trigger
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight. Answer = Trigger, or the vivid fact (the movie horse mounted rearing in a museum after death). Keep it light and concrete.

name: Egyptian Cats: The First House Pets
scope: Ancient Egypt gave us the earliest well-documented pet cats — welcomed for killing granary rats, then adored, painted in tomb art beside their owners' chairs, mourned by shaving one's eyebrows, and mummified in the millions.
source: Britannica: domestication of the cat; Egyptian tomb painting; Herodotus II
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = Egypt / the pet cat, or the vivid custom (mourning a dead cat by shaving your eyebrows). Keep the cat's move from pest-control to beloved pet the throughline; connects to the Bastet ladder but stays on pet-history here.

name: Cave Canem: Dogs of the Roman Household
scope: Rome kept dogs as pets and guardians — the famous 'Cave Canem' (Beware of the Dog) mosaic in a Pompeii doorway shows a chained hound, and a plaster cast preserves a Pompeii dog that died still on its chain. Small lapdogs appear on gravestones with loving epitaphs.
source: Britannica: dogs in the ancient world; Pompeii excavations; Roman epitaphs
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight. Answer = the Roman house dog / Cave Canem mosaic, or the vivid artifact (a 'Beware of the Dog' floor mosaic; a Pompeii dog cast still on its chain). Keep the animal-and-affection detail central.

name: Koi: Turning a Food Fish into Living Jewels
scope: Ornamental koi began when 19th-century rice farmers in Niigata, Japan, noticed color mutations in the common carp they raised for food and bred the brightest ones; the prize varieties (like the red-and-white Kohaku) can now sell for enormous sums and live for decades.
source: Britannica: koi; Niigata carp-breeding history
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight. Answer = koi, or the vivid origin (rice farmers breeding a food fish into living jewels). The food-to-ornament transformation is the hook.

name: The Victorian Cat Fancy and the First Cat Show
scope: Organized cat breeding began with the first great cat show at London's Crystal Palace in 1871, staged by Harrison Weir, who wrote the first breed 'points of excellence'; the show turned the ordinary cat into a fancy-bred, judged, ribboned animal.
source: Britannica: cat fancy; Harrison Weir, Our Cats and All About Them (1889)
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight. Answer = the 1871 Crystal Palace cat show / Harrison Weir, or the vivid turn (the first time cats were judged and ribboned like show animals). Avoid rote 'what year' framing — lead with the scene.

name: Westminster and Crufts: The Great Dog Shows
scope: The Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show, running since 1877, is one of America's oldest continuous sporting events; Britain's Crufts, founded by dog-biscuit salesman Charles Cruft in 1891, grew into the largest dog show on Earth. Both crown a single 'Best in Show.'
source: Britannica: Westminster Kennel Club; Crufts history
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight. Answer = the named show or the vivid origin (Crufts started by a dog-biscuit salesman). Keep the human-and-dog spectacle concrete; avoid pure date-drill.

name: Martin's Act and 'Humanity Dick'
scope: The world's first modern animal-cruelty law, the 1822 Cruel Treatment of Cattle Act, was pushed through Parliament by the eccentric Irish MP Richard Martin — 'Humanity Dick' — who then personally hauled a donkey-beater into court and brought the abused donkey in as evidence.
source: Britannica: Richard Martin; RSPCA founding history
framing_note: Scene-led, welfare-history figure told as a vivid person-and-animal story, not as statute clauses. Answer = 'Humanity Dick' Martin, or the vivid act (bringing the beaten donkey into the courtroom as a witness). Keep the animal in frame; don't drift into legislative text.

name: Henry Bergh and the Founding of the ASPCA
scope: A wealthy New Yorker who, sickened by seeing cart horses beaten in the street, founded the ASPCA in 1866 and got America's first effective anti-cruelty law; he patrolled the streets himself in a top hat, stopping drivers and even a live-turtle shipment. He later helped found the first child-protection society too.
source: Britannica: Henry Bergh; ASPCA founding history
framing_note: Scene-led, welfare-history figure as a vivid person-and-animal story. Answer = Bergh / the ASPCA, or the vivid act (a top-hatted man stopping horse-beaters in the street himself). Keep the animals and the person central, not the legal text.

name: Peter Singer and the Animal Liberation Argument
scope: The 1975 book Animal Liberation, which popularized the word 'speciesism' and argued from utilitarian ethics that an animal's capacity to suffer should count morally — becoming the philosophical spark of the modern animal-rights movement.
source: Britannica: Peter Singer; Animal Liberation (1975)
framing_note: Scene-led where possible; this is the ONE welfare topic that is an argument, not a story. STANCE: summarize Singer's utilitarian claim (suffering matters morally; 'speciesism') as a POSITION he holds — accurately, neither endorsed nor strawmanned. The bank does NOT adopt 'all animal use is wrong.' Answer = the named idea (speciesism / his suffering-based argument), attributed to Singer as a claim, not a verdict the stem imposes.

name: PETA and the Silver Spring Monkeys
scope: PETA, founded in 1980 by Ingrid Newkirk and Alex Pacheco, first drew national attention through the 1981 Silver Spring monkeys case — an undercover exposé of a research lab that became the first US police raid on an animal laboratory and a landmark legal fight.
source: Britannica: PETA; the Silver Spring monkeys case
framing_note: Scene-led, presented as the real cultural phenomenon it is — the founding and the Silver Spring case as fact, not as endorsement of PETA's positions. Answer = PETA / the Silver Spring monkeys, or the vivid fact (the first police raid on a US research lab over animal treatment). Report, don't preach.

name: Bullfighting: The Spanish Corrida and Its Bans
scope: The Spanish corrida de toros, its three formal acts (tercios) and the matador's cape and sword, presented as the tradition it is — alongside the fact that it has been banned in Catalonia (2010) and the Canary Islands, remains hugely contested, and defenders call it art while opponents call it cruelty.
source: Britannica: bullfighting; records of regional Spanish bans
framing_note: Scene-led wonder for the practice's form; STANCE: present both the tradition (its stages, its cultural weight) and the bans/objections factually, no preaching either way. Answer = the practice's named element (the corrida, the matador, a tercio) or the vivid contested fact (Catalonia's ban). Both sides framed.

name: Portuguese Bullfighting: The Horseman Who Doesn't Kill in the Ring
scope: In the Portuguese tourada, the star is the cavaleiro fighting from a superbly trained horse, and a team of forcados grabs the bull bare-handed; crucially, the bull is not killed in the arena (a legacy of an 18th-century royal ban on ring-killing), distinguishing it from the Spanish corrida.
source: Britannica: bullfighting (Portuguese tradition); tourada records
framing_note: Scene-led; present the distinction factually (horseback, bull not killed in-ring), both-sides on the wider debate. Answer = the Portuguese distinction (the cavaleiro on horseback; the bull spared in the arena). No preaching.

name: Cockfighting: An Ancient Sport, Now Widely Banned
scope: The pitting of gamecocks, one of the oldest spectator sports, recorded among the ancient Greeks and Persians and woven into cultures worldwide; it remains a legal, organized industry in some places (e.g., Philippine sabong) while being banned throughout the United States and much of the West.
source: Britannica: cockfighting; regional legality overviews
framing_note: Scene-led; present the practice's antiquity and reach plus its banned status factually, no preaching. Answer = cockfighting / a named tradition (sabong) or the vivid historical fact. Both sides framed neutrally.

name: Dog Fighting: From the Vick Case to a Felony Nationwide
scope: Dog fighting, descended from old bull- and bear-baiting blood sports, is now a felony in all fifty US states; the 2007 case of NFL quarterback Michael Vick's Bad Newz Kennels brought national attention and led to the rehabilitation of many of the seized dogs.
source: Britannica: dog fighting; coverage of the 2007 Vick case
framing_note: Scene-led; present the practice and its illegality factually. Answer = the vivid fact (a felony in all 50 states; the Vick case and the rehab of the seized dogs). Report; no preaching, but the illegality is simply a fact to state.

name: Fox Hunting and the 2004 Ban
scope: The traditional English mounted fox hunt — red coats, a pack of hounds, and the horn — presented as the ritual it was, alongside the 2004 Hunting Act that banned hunting wild mammals with dogs in England and Wales; 'drag hunting' (following a laid scent) continues legally.
source: Britannica: fox hunting; UK Hunting Act 2004
framing_note: Scene-led; present the tradition and the ban factually, both sides of a genuinely contested cultural fight. Answer = the fox hunt / the 2004 ban / drag hunting as the legal successor. No preaching.

name: The Kentucky Derby: The Run for the Roses
scope: America's oldest continuously held sporting event, run since 1875 on the first Saturday in May at Churchill Downs; the winner is draped in a garland of over 400 roses, giving it the nickname 'the Run for the Roses,' and the whole spectacle lasts about two minutes.
source: Britannica: Kentucky Derby; Churchill Downs history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the Kentucky Derby, or the vivid detail (a garland of 400+ roses; 'the most exciting two minutes in sports'). Keep the horse and the spectacle central, not a date-drill.

name: Secretariat and the 31-Length Belmont
scope: The chestnut colt who ended a 25-year Triple Crown drought in 1973 and won the Belmont Stakes by an astonishing 31 lengths in a record time that still stands; a later autopsy found his heart weighed roughly two-and-a-half times a normal horse's.
source: Britannica: Secretariat; 1973 Triple Crown records
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = Secretariat, or the vivid fact (winning the Belmont by 31 lengths; a heart two-and-a-half times normal size). The oversized heart is the Dinner-Test payoff.

name: The Triple Crown of Horse Racing
scope: The three races a colt must sweep in a single season — the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness Stakes, and the Belmont Stakes — a feat so hard that only a handful of horses have ever done it, with a famous 37-year gap before American Pharoah broke through in 2015.
source: Britannica: Triple Crown (horse racing); race records
framing_note: Scene-led. Answer = the Triple Crown / a named race, or the vivid fact (the decades-long droughts between winners). Lead with the difficulty and the drama, not a list.

name: Polo, the Sport of Kings from Persia
scope: One of the oldest team sports, born in ancient Persia (chovgan) around the 6th century BC as cavalry training, spread through India, and carried worldwide by the British; players switch ponies between chukkas because the game is so hard on the mounts.
source: Britannica: polo; Persian and British-Indian history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = polo, or the vivid origin (Persian cavalry training that became the sport of kings). The pony-swapping between chukkas is a good concrete handle.

name: Dressage: The Highest Expression of Horse Training
scope: The Olympic discipline in which horse and rider perform precise, dance-like movements from nearly invisible cues, its roots in classical cavalry academies like the Spanish Riding School of Vienna and its Lipizzaner stallions performing 'airs above the ground.'
source: Britannica: dressage; Spanish Riding School of Vienna
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = dressage, or the vivid image (Lipizzaner stallions leaping in the 'airs above the ground' from invisible cues). Keep the horse's trained artistry central.

name: The Iditarod and the Trail It Honors
scope: The ~1,000-mile Anchorage-to-Nome sled dog race, founded by Joe Redington Sr. in 1973, run to keep alive the memory of the 1925 serum run and the sled-dog tradition itself; teams and mushers cross Alaskan wilderness in deep winter over roughly two weeks.
source: Britannica: Iditarod; 1925 serum-run commemoration
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the Iditarod, or the vivid link (a 1,000-mile race founded to honor the sled dogs of the 1925 serum run). Connects to the Balto/Togo ladder; keep the dogs central. Racing-welfare debate can be touched factually if it arises, but the focus is the animals and the tradition.

name: Falconry: The Feathered Rank of Kings
scope: The ancient art of hunting with trained birds of prey, named a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage; in the medieval 'Boke of St Albans' a strict pecking order matched bird to rank — an eagle for an emperor, a gyrfalcon for a king, a peregrine for a prince, down to a kestrel for a servant.
source: Britannica: falconry; the Boke of St Albans; UNESCO Intangible Heritage listing
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = falconry / the named bird-to-rank match (the king's gyrfalcon), or the vivid fact (a medieval law of which bird your rank could fly). The rank-by-raptor table is a great Dinner-Test hook.

name: Mongol Horse Archers: An Empire on Horseback
scope: The Mongol warrior's bond with the small tough steppe horse — each rider led three to five remounts so he could ride for days, drank fermented mare's milk (airag), and could loose arrows accurately at a gallop by shooting in the instant all four hooves left the ground.
source: Britannica: Mongol military; steppe cavalry history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, told straight. Answer = the Mongol horse / horse archer, or the vivid technique (firing arrows in the split second all four hooves are off the ground; multiple remounts giving unmatched range). Keep the horse-and-rider partnership central.

name: The Destrier, the Medieval Knight's Warhorse
scope: The prized heavy warhorse of the mounted knight, trained to charge and to bite and kick in the melee, and to bear an armored rider; ancestors of today's Shire and Percheron drafts, destriers were so valuable they cost many times an ordinary horse.
source: Britannica: destrier / medieval warhorse; equestrian history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the destrier, or the vivid fact (a warhorse trained to bite and kick in battle, worth a fortune). Keep the animal and the partnership central, not just armor.

name: The Pony Express and the Race Against the Telegraph
scope: The relay of fast horses and light riders that carried mail across ~1,900 miles from Missouri to California in about ten days in 1860-61; riders changed to a fresh horse every 10-15 miles, and the whole enterprise lasted barely 18 months before the transcontinental telegraph made it obsolete.
source: Britannica: Pony Express; American West history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, told straight. Answer = the Pony Express, or the vivid fact (a fresh horse every 10-15 miles, coast to coast in ten days, killed off by the telegraph in 18 months). Keep the horses and the relay central.

name: The Guide Dog: From Blinded Veterans to the Seeing Eye
scope: Systematic guide-dog training began in Germany after WWI to help soldiers blinded by gas; the idea reached America through Dorothy Harrison Eustis and the young blind man Morris Frank, whose German shepherd Buddy led him across a busy street to prove it, launching the Seeing Eye school in 1929.
source: Britannica: guide dog; The Seeing Eye founding history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight. Answer = the guide dog / Buddy the shepherd, or the vivid proof (a blind man crossing a dangerous street behind his dog to show America it worked). Keep the dog-and-person partnership central.

name: Military Working Dogs and Cairo of the bin Laden Raid
scope: Modern military working dogs — most often Belgian Malinois and German shepherds — sniff out explosives, clear buildings, and jump from aircraft with their handlers; a Malinois named Cairo accompanied the 2011 SEAL raid that killed Osama bin Laden, the most famous of them.
source: Britannica: military working dogs; reporting on the 2011 raid
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight. Answer = the military working dog / Cairo the Malinois, or the vivid fact (a dog on the bin Laden raid; dogs that parachute strapped to their handlers). Keep the working partnership central.

name: Saint Bernards and the Monks of the Alpine Pass
scope: The great rescue dogs bred by monks at the Great St Bernard Pass in the Alps to find travelers buried in snow; the most famous, Barry, is credited with saving dozens of lives around 1800. The brandy-keg collar of legend was a Victorian artist's invention.
source: Britannica: Saint Bernard (dog); Great St Bernard Hospice history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight — including debunking the brandy-keg myth honestly. Answer = the Saint Bernard / Barry, or the vivid fact (a monastery dog credited with dozens of alpine rescues; the brandy keg was never real). The myth-vs-fact twist is the payoff.

name: Medical Detection Dogs: Noses That Smell Disease
scope: Dogs trained to detect illness by scent — sniffing out certain cancers from breath or samples, alerting a diabetic to a dangerous blood-sugar drop, or warning of an oncoming seizure minutes before it strikes; some were trained to screen for COVID-19 by smell.
source: Britannica / Medical Detection Dogs (UK); Penn Vet Working Dog Center research
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight (framed as documented capability, not miracle). Answer = the detection dog / the named feat (smelling cancer; alerting before a seizure). Keep the animal's extraordinary nose central; ties to the dog-olfaction biology in Pillar 1.

name: Service Animals and the Law That Names Them
scope: The working service dog — a guide dog for the blind, a mobility or seizure-alert dog — trained to do specific tasks for a person with a disability; under US law such a dog goes where its person goes, a protection that (importantly) does not extend the same way to emotional-support animals.
source: Britannica: service animal; Americans with Disabilities Act definition
framing_note: Scene-led, kept about the ANIMAL and its trained task, not statute clauses. Answer = the service dog / its trained task (guiding, alerting), or the vivid distinction (a task-trained service dog vs. a comfort animal). Touch the legal definition only as it frames the working dog; don't drift into law-drill.

name: Set and the Chaos Beast of the Desert
scope: The red-haired god of storms, the desert, and disorder, shown with the head of an unidentified 'Set animal' (a curved snout and squared ears matching no living creature); he murdered his brother Osiris and warred endlessly with Horus for the throne.
source: Britannica: Set (Seth); Pinch, Egyptian Mythology
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight (Set as chaos, not simple 'evil'). Answer = Set, or the vivid mystery (a god with the head of an animal no one can identify). The unknown 'Set animal' is the hook.

name: Khepri, the Scarab Who Rolls the Sun
scope: The dung beetle rolls its ball across the sand as the god Khepri rolls the sun across the sky each dawn; because young beetles seemed to emerge from the ball alone, the scarab became the great Egyptian symbol of self-renewal, carved as amulets over the heart of mummies.
source: Britannica: scarab; Pinch, Egyptian Mythology
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = the scarab / Khepri, or the vivid link (a beetle rolling dung = a god rolling the sun; the heart-scarab amulet of rebirth). Keep it concrete.

name: The Chimera, the Fire-Breathing Mash-Up
scope: A single monster fused from three animals - a lion in front, a goat rising from its back, and a serpent for a tail - breathing fire; Bellerophon killed it from the air on Pegasus by ramming a block of lead down its throat, which its own flame melted.
source: Britannica: Chimera; Homer, Iliad VI; Apollodorus, Library
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the Chimera, or the clever kill (melting lead down its throat with its own fire). Ties to the Pegasus ladder; keep the three-animal image vivid.

name: The Sphinx and Her Deadly Riddle
scope: The winged lion with a woman's head who strangled travelers outside Thebes until one solved her riddle - what walks on four legs at dawn, two at noon, and three at dusk; Oedipus answered 'a human,' and the Sphinx threw herself from her rock.
source: Britannica: Sphinx (Greek); Sophocles, Oedipus Rex; Apollodorus
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the Sphinx, or the vivid riddle and its answer ('a human,' who crawls, walks, then uses a cane). Distinguish the Greek Sphinx from the Egyptian one. Keep the riddle central.

name: The Phoenix, the Bird Reborn from Its Ashes
scope: The fabulous bird of Greek and Egyptian (Bennu) legend that lives for centuries, builds a nest of aromatic spices, burns itself to ash, and rises again young from the fire; only one exists at a time. It became a lasting symbol of resurrection and renewal.
source: Britannica: phoenix; Herodotus II; the Egyptian Bennu
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, both Greek and Egyptian roots on the same plane. Answer = the phoenix, or the vivid cycle (burning itself to ash and rising young again). Note the Egyptian Bennu link as context.

name: The Griffin, Guardian of Gold
scope: The beast with the body of a lion and the head, wings, and talons of an eagle - a fusion of the king of beasts and the king of birds; ancient writers placed griffins in the mountains of Scythia, guarding hoards of gold and fighting the one-eyed Arimaspians who tried to steal it.
source: Britannica: griffin; Herodotus; Aelian, On Animals
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = the griffin, or the vivid image (lion-eagle guardian of gold in the mountains). Keep the treasure-guarding role concrete.

name: Actaeon and the Hounds That Turned on Their Master
scope: The hunter Actaeon stumbled on the goddess Artemis bathing; in fury she turned him into a stag, and his own pack of hunting hounds, no longer knowing their master, chased him down and tore him apart. A myth about the animals turned against the man.
source: Britannica: Actaeon; Ovid, Metamorphoses III
framing_note: Scene-led wonder. Answer = Actaeon's own hounds, or the vivid horror (a hunter turned to a stag and killed by his own dogs). Keep the animal reversal central.

name: The Unicorn: From Rhino Rumor to Tapestry
scope: The one-horned beast, described by ancient writers (perhaps from garbled rhino or oryx reports) and cast in medieval Christian allegory as a symbol of purity that only a maiden could tame; the famous 'Hunt of the Unicorn' tapestries read it as an image of Christ.
source: Britannica: unicorn; the Cloisters 'Hunt of the Unicorn' tapestries; medieval bestiaries
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, Christian allegory on the same plane as other traditions. Answer = the unicorn, or the vivid lore (only a maiden could tame it; the tapestry hunt read as Christ). Present the belief as held; note the possible rhino/oryx origin.

name: Saint Jerome and the Lion with a Thorn
scope: The legend that a great lion limped into Saint Jerome's monastery and, instead of fleeing, the scholar-saint drew a thorn from its paw; the grateful lion stayed as his loyal companion, and painters ever after show Jerome with a lion at his feet.
source: Britannica: Saint Jerome; The Golden Legend; hagiographic tradition
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, tradition straight. Answer = Jerome's lion, or the vivid act (a saint pulling a thorn from a lion's paw, winning its loyalty). Told as the saint's legend.

name: The White Elephant, Sacred Beast of Buddhist Kings
scope: In Hindu and Buddhist tradition a rare albino elephant is a sign of royal blessing; the Buddha's mother dreamed a white elephant entered her side before his birth, and Southeast Asian kings kept sacred white elephants - a gift so costly to maintain it could ruin a rival, the origin of the phrase 'white elephant.'
source: Britannica: white elephant; Buddhist birth legend; Thai/Burmese royal tradition
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, Hindu/Buddhist tradition straight and on the same plane. Answer = the sacred white elephant, or the vivid link (a queen's dream of a white elephant; the ruinous royal gift behind the English idiom).

name: Old Drum and 'A Dog Is a Man's Best Friend'
scope: A Missouri farmer's beloved hound, Old Drum, was shot in 1869; at the trial lawyer George Graham Vest gave a 'Eulogy of the Dog' so moving - 'the one absolutely unselfish friend a man can have' - that it won the case and gave the world the phrase about a dog being man's best friend.
source: Britannica / Missouri legal history; Vest's 'Eulogy of the Dog' (1870)
framing_note: Scene-led, true story straight. Answer = Old Drum, or the vivid origin (a courtroom eulogy for a shot hound gave us 'man's best friend'). Keep the dog and the speech central.

name: Clever Hans, the Horse Who 'Did Math'
scope: A German horse around 1900 that seemed to answer arithmetic by tapping his hoof - until psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed Hans was reading tiny unconscious cues in the questioner's posture, stopping when the human relaxed; the 'Clever Hans effect' still warns every animal-cognition experiment.
source: Britannica: Clever Hans; Pfungst's 1907 study
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight - the twist is the real lesson (the horse read body language, not numbers). Answer = Clever Hans, or the vivid reveal (he was reading the human's cues, not doing math). Not mockery - the horse was genuinely perceptive.

name: Jumbo, the Elephant Who Named 'Jumbo'
scope: The enormous African elephant of the London Zoo, beloved by Victorian children who rode on his back, sold to P.T. Barnum's circus amid public outcry in 1882; his name - possibly from Swahili - became the English word for anything huge. He was killed by a train in 1885.
source: Britannica: Jumbo (elephant); London Zoo and Barnum records
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, true story straight (including the sad end, told soberly). Answer = Jumbo, or the vivid fact (an elephant so famous his name became the word for 'huge'). Keep the animal central.

name: The Tower's Polar Bear: Beasts of the Royal Menagerie
scope: Medieval kings kept menageries as living treasures and diplomatic gifts - the Tower of London housed lions, a polar bear that fished in the Thames on a long chain (a gift from Norway, ~1252), and an elephant sent by the King of France to Henry III in 1255, the first elephant England had seen.
source: Britannica: Royal Menagerie / Tower of London; Matthew Paris chronicle
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, told straight. Answer = the royal menagerie / the Tower's polar bear or elephant, or the vivid image (a polar bear fishing in the Thames on a chain). Keep the animals central.

name: Rodeo and the American Working Cowboy
scope: Rodeo grew out of the real skills of Spanish-Mexican vaqueros and American ranch cowboys - roping, bronc-riding, and cutting cattle - turned into contest; its events like bull riding and barrel racing preserve, and dramatize, the horsemanship of the working range.
source: Britannica: rodeo; vaquero and ranching history
framing_note: Scene-led wonder, told straight; the welfare debate around rodeo can be noted factually if it arises but the focus is the horsemanship and working roots. Answer = rodeo / a named event or the vaquero origin. Keep horse and rider central.

name: Carrier Pigeons and the Message That Beat the Telegraph
scope: Long before radio, homing pigeons carried news faster than any horse - Reuters began partly as a pigeon service, and besieged Paris in 1870 flew microfilmed dispatches out by pigeon; a bird's uncanny ability to find home over hundreds of miles made it a genuine military and news technology.
source: Britannica: homing pigeon; Siege of Paris 1870; Reuters early history
